info.title: Two Minute Billing API
info.description:
Multi-tenant subscription billing. Account hierarchy: Organization → Business → Customer → Subscription. Authenticate with `Authorization: Bearer <api_key>`; every write accepts an `Idempotency-Key`. Money is integer minor units + ISO currency.

**Unknown parameters.** A body or query key the endpoint does not define — at any depth — answers **400** `invalid_request_error` with `message: "Unknown parameter: <path>"` (e.g. `items[0].qty`) and `param` naming the first one; nothing is written. Values inside `metadata` and `custom_fields`, and top-level `cf_<name>` custom-field keys, are free-form.

**Rate limits.** Requests are counted per API key in fixed one-minute windows. Every authenticated response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` (unix seconds, when the window and the allowance reset), so a client can back off before it is refused. Over the limit answers **429** with `error.type = "rate_limit_error"` and a `Retry-After` header in seconds — wait that long rather than retrying immediately. The ceiling applies per key, so an organization's integrations do not consume each other's allowance; it is set per organization, so ask us to raise it rather than sharding across keys. A 429 means nothing was processed: the request is safe to retry unchanged, and with an `Idempotency-Key` it is safe to retry even if you are unsure. Some actions also have their own, tighter limit (team invites, webhook resends and test sends, ad hoc emails, invoice collect/retry, checkout coupon codes); the 429 message names it.

**List filtering.** Paginated lists filter with `<field>[<op>]=<value>` — e.g. `?created_at[after]=2026-09-01&status[in]=paid,posted`. There is no `filters` parameter: each filterable field is documented as its own query parameter, and any query key that is neither a filter nor a documented one is a **400** rather than a silently ignored no-op. Most operators take one scalar; four do not — `in`/`not_in` take a comma-separated set, `between` exactly two comma-separated values (both ends inclusive), `in_last`/`in_next` a positive number of DAYS, and `is_present` takes `true` or `false`. Dates are ISO-8601. Sorting is `sort_by[asc]=<field>` or `sort_by[desc]=<field>`.

**Request ids.** Every response carries a `Request-Id` header (`req_…`). Requests your API keys make, and writes made in the dashboard, are kept in the request log: open one with `GET /v1/request_logs/{id}` to see what was sent and what was answered. Reads are kept 30 days, writes 90 days.

tags.name: Organization
tags.description: Your account, and the boundary nothing crosses. An organization holds the API keys and owns every business under it; no request authenticated with your key can reach another organization's data, and nothing you create is visible outside it.

tags.name: Analytics
tags.description:
The measures behind every board and chart, as one read. `GET /v1/analytics/measures` describes the whole space so nothing has to be hard-coded; `GET /v1/analytics` answers one measure over one window, optionally split by one dimension; `POST /v1/analytics/query` answers a board's worth in one round trip.

Every payload is self-describing, because a number without its unit is a bug waiting to happen: it states its unit and currency (money is integer MINOR units, never converted here), whether it is a value AT an instant or a sum OVER a window, when it was computed, and — where the history is only partly known — exactly which periods are missing. A cut that cannot be made answers 422 with a sentence naming what can.

tags.name: Businesses
tags.description:
A business is an independent book inside your organization: its own catalogue, its own currencies, its own payment gateways, its own customers. Two businesses share nothing but the account they belong to, which is how one organization sells under several brands or in several countries without their data or their numbering ever mixing.

Each business has a **live mode and a test mode**: two business ids, created together. The test mode (`test_business_id` on the live business) starts as a copy of the live settings and is independent after that; move catalog and settings between them with a configuration transfer. Test keys reach only test mode and live keys only live mode. Test mode is where you rehearse: it can seed sample data, its Time Travel moves a simulated clock forward so you can watch a year of renewals, dunning and expiry in minutes, it sends email only to your team members, and nothing it produces reaches a live webhook endpoint.

tags.name: Catalog
tags.description:
What you sell, in three layers. A **product** is the thing (a plan, an add-on, a one-off charge); a **price** is an amount in one currency on one billing period; a **product group** organises products for reporting. A subscription is always bought at a price, never at a product, which is what lets the same plan cost different amounts in different currencies.

**Editing a price does not reprice anybody.** A change applies to new subscriptions only — existing ones keep the price they were sold at until you change them explicitly. Archiving is soft throughout and never touches a subscription already using the item; it only stops the item being chosen again.

Coupons live here too, either as a single reusable code or as a **coupon set** of bulk unique single-use codes.

tags.name: Customers
tags.description:
The payer: who they are, where they are (which decides their tax), and what they are owed.

A customer can carry money in three distinct forms, and they are not interchangeable. **Promotional credit** is goodwill you granted — it reduces invoices and is never refundable. **Excess payment** is real money they overpaid, held until an invoice needs it. A **wallet** is prepaid balance, which may have been paid for or granted. An invoice draws on them in a fixed order, so the same total settles the same way every time.

Archiving a customer is soft and reversible. `clear_personal_data` is not: it redacts the personal fields in place for erasure requests and detaches every vaulted instrument. The ledger, invoices and payments are left intact — the ledger is append-only and the numbers still have to add up.

tags.name: Payment Methods
tags.description:
A stored instrument and the gateway it lives at. **We never hold a card number** — the gateway vaults it and returns a token, which is what these endpoints manage. Some instruments need the buyer to approve the mandate first; `setup` begins that flow and the vault completes it once they have.

An instrument carries a **role**, not just a default flag. Collection tries the subscription's own method first, then the customer's primary, then their backup if the primary HARD-declines — so a dead card does not have to become a failed renewal. A soft, retriable decline is not a fallback: it is retried on the same instrument.

**Gateway accounts** are also here — the connections themselves, their credential verification, and provisioning the notification endpoint the gateway calls back on. A business can hold several and route by currency and method type.

tags.name: Subscriptions
tags.description:
The engine owns subscription state. A gateway charges and refunds; what a subscription IS, when it renews and what it costs is decided here, so nothing changes underneath you when a provider does.

**Every money-moving operation has an estimate that does not move money.** `estimate`, `cancel_estimate`, `reactivate_estimate`, `renewal_estimate` and `subscription_estimate` return the exact proration, tax and credit the real call would produce. Show one to a customer before you charge them.

Two ways to change items, and picking the wrong one is the usual mistake. `change` applies a **delta** — these items added, those removed. `update_for_items` reconciles against a **desired final set** and removes anything absent from it. A delta sent to the second endpoint deletes everything you did not mention.

Anything dated can be scheduled instead of applied: cancel, pause, resume and change all take a future date, and a pending schedule can be listed and withdrawn before it fires.

tags.name: Invoices
tags.description:
An invoice is money owed, and its history is append-only — which is why there are three different ways to end one and they are not alternatives. **Void** reverses an invoice raised in error, undoing its postings and refunding anything applied. **Write off** accepts that a real debt will not be paid and books it as bad debt. A **credit note** reduces what is owed, or returns money, while the invoice itself stands.

A pending invoice is still being assembled; `close` finalizes it, applying discounts, tax and available credit, and that is the point it becomes payable. Collection can be triggered by hand and dunning can be paused or stopped per invoice when you are negotiating.

Refunds are grouped here because a refund follows a credit note: issue one against the invoice, then return the money to the card, or record that you returned it some other way.

tags.name: Entitlements
tags.description:
What a plan actually unlocks, so your product can ask the billing system instead of keeping its own copy of who bought what. A **feature** is a switch, a quota or a meter; attaching one to a product grants it to every subscription of that product.

A subscription's effective entitlements are the plan's grants **overlaid with any overrides set on that subscription**, so a one-off arrangement for a single customer does not need a private plan. `check` answers the runtime question — is this subscription entitled, and to how much.

tags.name: Integrations
tags.description: Connect a business to another tool. `GET /v1/integrations` lists every integration and what it needs. A **push** integration (an affiliate program, for example) is connected with its credentials through the routes below: each matching billing event becomes one call to the partner, retried with backoff, with a delivery log per connection. A **sync** integration (HubSpot) has its own routes.

tags.name: HubSpot
tags.description: Keep customers in sync with a HubSpot portal. A business connects once through HubSpot's install screen; after that every change is pushed within a minute while autosync is on, and a full sync runs every 15 minutes. Each run and every record it touched is on the sync log.

tags.name: Webhooks
tags.description:
The endpoints below MANAGE subscriptions; what follows is what arrives at one.

**The envelope.** Every delivery is a `POST` of exactly these eight fields, and no others: `id` (the event id, also sent as a header), `occurred_at`, `source`, `user` (the actor, when one is known), `event_type`, `api_version`, `content` and `object: "event"`. `content` nests the resource under its own type — `{ invoice: { id, …, resource_version } }` — so one shape parses every event.

**Verify the signature before you trust a delivery.** `Tmbilling-Signature` is `sha256=` followed by the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the RAW request body, keyed with that endpoint's signing secret. Compute it over the bytes you received, not over a re-serialised object — re-encoding JSON changes the bytes and the digest with them. Compare with a constant-time equality. `Tmbilling-Event-Id` repeats the event id so you can dedupe without parsing the body; treat it as the idempotency key for your own side, because a redelivery reuses it.

**Delivery and retries.** Any 2xx is success. Anything else is retried up to 6 attempts with a fixed backoff — 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 6h — after which the delivery is marked failed and left for you to redeliver. A host that stops answering is circuit-broken: deliveries to it are held rather than attempted, and those pauses cost none of the 6 attempts. Deliveries are not ordered; use `occurred_at` if order matters to you.

**What an endpoint receives.** An endpoint with no `event_types` receives every type, including ones added after you created it; set `event_types` to receive only those. An endpoint scoped to a business receives only that business's events, and an endpoint always stays inside its own test/live partition — a test business's activity never reaches a production consumer. Events about the organization itself belong to no business and reach both partitions.

tags.name: Payment Intents
tags.description: A payment intent is a CONTAINER of attempts at a gateway, for one of two purposes. `payment` authorizes a priced charge that is later captured INTO an invoice; `setup` is a ZERO-amount authorization whose product is a vaulted instrument (Stripe `seti_…`) and which moves no money. Each try at the gateway is a `payment_attempt`: a buyer who fails 3DS twice before succeeding leaves three attempts, and none of the earlier ones are overwritten.

tags.name: Custom Fields
tags.description:
Your own fields on our records, defined per business so each book keeps its own vocabulary. A definition sets the label, the type and whether a value is required.

Values filter through the ordinary list grammar as `cf_<api_name>`, e.g. `?cf_plan_tier[is]=gold`, and are resolved per request from that business's definitions — which is why they cannot be listed as fixed query parameters on the list endpoints. Archiving a definition is soft and leaves existing values in place.

tags.name: Report dashboards
tags.description: A named, saved arrangement of reports. A dashboard stores REFERENCES to report keys plus the options each tile pins — never a copy of a report definition — so a tile cannot drift from the report it names. Org-level with an optional `business`, the same shape as list views and for the same reason. `visibility` decides who sees one; only the owner may rename, re-share, default or delete it. A key can leave the catalogue, so a tile carries `available` and is reported as unavailable rather than silently dropped — a dashboard that quietly loses a tile changes what its name means.

tags.name: List views
tags.description: A saved way of looking at one list — a segment. It holds the filters, free-text search, sort and column choice, and its `filters` use exactly the `?<field>[<op>]=<value>` grammar the list endpoints take, so a stored view and a live API call say the same thing. Scoped to an `entity` (which list) and, for all but the two org-wide lists, a business. `visibility` decides who SEES a view; only its owner may ever change one, and `duplicate` is how you make a colleague's shared view yours.

tags.name: Reference
tags.description: Country reference data — the ISO 3166 lists the address contract validates against. UNAUTHENTICATED, because hosted checkout and the customer portal render the same address form under a short-lived buyer token rather than an org API key. Cacheable for a day.

tags.name: Tax
tags.description:
Tax is configured per **region**, and a region is a country you have registered in. Within it, rates are a **component vector** rather than one number, because a single sale can attract several taxes at once that must appear separately on the invoice.

A **tax profile** applies one class of rate to one class of product, so reduced-rate and standard-rate goods can sit in the same catalogue. Where a sale is taxed depends on the place of supply — the buyer's address against the seller's registrations — so state registrations are held per region and snapshotted onto each invoice. A region can be priced tax-inclusive, in which case the tax is backed out of the price rather than added to it.

tags.name: Payments
tags.description:
What happens when a gateway says no. Every decline a provider can return is mapped to a canonical answer: whether it is worth retrying, whether the instrument should be marked unusable, and what the customer should be told.

The built-in mapping is the default, and a business can override it at two levels — one specific gateway rule, or every rule producing one canonical code. Deleting an override restores the built-in answer rather than removing the handling.

tags.name: Payment Instructions
tags.description:
How to pay you without a card. Each instruction is a block of plain-text label and value pairs — bank name, account number, reference — that is rendered onto the customer-facing invoice PDF and HTML.

Plain text on both halves deliberately: this lands on a document you send to customers, so no markup is accepted. Archiving is soft, and invoices already issued keep the instructions they were rendered with.

tags.name: Payment Links
tags.description: Reusable public links for your website: a buy button for a one-time product, or a subscribe button for a plan. Each visitor gets their own checkout, so one link serves any number of buyers. Archive a link to stop it; its past checkouts are kept.

tags.name: Reason Codes
tags.description:
The list an operator picks from when cancelling, refunding or writing something off. Recording a stable code rather than free prose is what makes churn and refund reporting groupable — "too expensive" typed five different ways counts as five reasons.

Lists are per business and per action, so a cancellation reason set is separate from a refund one.

tags.name: Dunning Policies
tags.description: Named dunning settings. A business keeps several and assigns one per customer (the customer's `dunning_policy`); a customer with none uses the business dunning settings. A customer excluded from dunning stays excluded whatever the policy.

tags.name: Receipts
tags.description: A numbered record of money received: one per payment, or one per payment-request payment. Numbers run in one series per business and are assigned within seconds of the payment. A receipt is not a tax invoice and never changes after it is created.

tags.name: Payment Requests
tags.description: Ask a customer for several open invoices at once: one charge for the total, or one link they pay once. Credit on file is applied first, then the money is applied to the invoices in the business's order (`billing_rules_config.payment_application.invoice_order`; default oldest due first). `origin` says who asked: `manual` (operator or API), `dunning` (the clock's combined retry) or `portal` (the customer). Each invoice gets its own payment, so refunds and credit notes work per invoice.

tags.name: Comments
tags.description: Operator notes attached to a record — a customer, a subscription, an invoice. Context for the next person who opens it, kept with the record instead of in someone's inbox. Comments are internal and never appear on anything a customer sees.

tags.name: Transfers
tags.description:
Copy catalogue configuration from one business into another: products with their prices, attached items and differential prices, or coupons. For standing up a second book that should sell what the first one sells without rebuilding it by hand.

A copy, not a link — the objects are independent once transferred, and editing one afterwards does not change the other.

tags.name: Usage
tags.description:
Send usage events from your app and bill them through meters. An event names a customer by any key your app already has (a user, workspace or API key id) or by the customer id. Its own `key` makes every send safe to retry: a repeat is a duplicate and counts once.

A **meter** says what to count: an event name, an aggregation, optional filters and up to five group-by properties. A **price** on the meter bills each combination of group values from a rate card with a default rate, at up to 12 decimal places, or passes through the event's own amount or cost plus a markup. Usage closes about 6 minutes after a period ends; an event that arrives later bills on the next invoice as usage from its own period.

tags.name: Model prices
tags.description:
A dated price list for AI models (model × token type), refreshed every hour from the public genai-prices list (MIT license) into a table we keep. Prices are USD. Each row has two dates: `source_effective_from`, the source's own date, and `effective_from`, the instant we apply it from. A change never reprices usage recorded before it. Every usage line that bills from the list cites the row it used (`mpr_…`), and you can get that row here.

**Your cost** is the price your organization pays its model provider. It feeds cost and margin, and is the markup base when a price asks for it. The sync never changes it.

tags.name: Credits
tags.description: Credit grants: money or your own unit of credit, given as promotional credit or sold as paid credit. Grants pay usage lines on invoices in a fixed order, expire, and keep every change as a credit transaction.

tags.name: Usage controls
tags.description: Keep spend in check and bill usage early: spend limits that the access check enforces, alerts with a state per threshold, credit runway, automatic top-up, invoices raised when unbilled usage reaches an amount, a preview of a rate change on real usage, and an embeddable usage widget for your own app.

post.summary: Send a usage event
post.description: The event's `key` makes the call safe to retry: a repeat key returns the stored event with status `duplicate` and changes nothing, even if its timestamp or values differ. Keys are kept 35 days. The `Idempotency-Key` header is not used. The event is stored before we answer. An event whose customer key matches no customer is kept as unmatched and bills once you add the key to a customer. Needs `usage_events:manage`.

post.summary: Mint a hosted-checkout session (subscribe, or change an existing subscription)
post.description: Returns a short-lived bearer token (returned exactly once) and the /checkout/s/<token> link a BUYER opens; the org API key never reaches their browser. mode='create' (default) subscribes a new customer to the items. mode='change' requires `subscription` and, on completion, upserts the items onto THAT subscription (plan swap / quantity change / add-ons) and applies the coupons. In change mode the customer is pinned to the subscription's owner at mint time and cannot be reassigned by the buyer. Items and coupons are validated AT MINT (a bogus price or coupon 404s here rather than failing the buyer mid-flow). A change session may carry only coupons; a create session needs at least one item. Unlisted items on the target are left alone unless replace_items_list is true. With reactivate:true a change session targets a CANCELLED subscription and completing it reactivates it with a fresh term, billed on the spot; a failed charge refuses it when the business requires a successful charge to reactivate.

delete.description: Removes the subscription from the account. To close the term out properly, cancel it instead. Everything it produced is kept and stays on the customer — invoices, payments and their ledger entries — and an unpaid invoice remains payable and stays in dunning. Reads of a deleted subscription return 404 and it no longer appears in lists.

post.summary: Reconcile a subscription against a DESIRED item list
post.description: Where `…/change` speaks in DELTAS against item ids the caller must already know, this takes the desired end state ("plan X plus two of add-on Y") and works out the swap/quantity/add/remove mix itself — so an integrator holding a configuration does not have to read the subscription, diff it, and re-implement that logic client-side. Non-interactive by design: the API sibling of the change-mode checkout, for a caller acting on the customer's behalf rather than a buyer at a page. It takes no payment.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Safely retry writes — repeats return the original response. If a write FAILED after it had already taken effect, that failure is what repeats: the key is spent, and a new attempt needs a new key.

items.description: The DESIRED items, not a delta. Anything already on the subscription and absent here is left alone unless replace_items_list or mandatory_items_to_remove says otherwise.

price.description: The price's id (a slug id, e.g. `pro-monthly-usd`).

replace_items_list.description: Treat `items` as exhaustive and drop unlisted NON-PLAN items.

mandatory_items_to_remove.description: Drop these PRICE ids whatever the mode.

prorate.description: False suppresses the credit/charge a mid-term change would raise — what a TRIAL upgrade needs, since nothing should be charged before the trial converts. There is no separate no-proration mode: false is applied by deferring the money (invoice_immediately=false), and how callers send it. Omitted → the engine's normal proration.

invoice_immediately.description: Where any prorated charge lands. Ignored when prorate=false. Omitted resolves the business setting `default_invoice_immediately`, as /change does.

reset_term.description: Restart the term at this change rather than keeping the current period boundary.

metadata.description: Metadata — REPLACED wholesale, and applied inside this change's own transaction so it commits with the item operations or not at all. For an edit where the items and a flag are one decision (a destination switch bills for one thing and serves what this names): landing them separately means the customer pays for one and receives the other. null clears; omit to leave it untouched.

200.description: Reconciled. The FULL subscription — items, customer, discount and default payment method, exactly as `GET /subscriptions/{sub}` returns it — plus `applied`: `changed` / `added` counts and the `removed` price ids, so a caller can assert what actually happened instead of diffing the subscription (a removal the mandatory-items guard REFUSED would otherwise look identical to one that was never requested). `items` is included because it is what this endpoint changed; it was omitted until 2026-09-08, which left callers re-reading the subscription to see the result of their own write.

400.description: The desired list could not be reconciled (unknown price, a removal that cannot be credited, or an invalid option combination)

409.description: A concurrent write invalidated the proration this change priced — retry; or the Idempotency-Key was reused with a different payload

post.summary: Record a metered usage event
post.description:
Send an `Idempotency-Key` header or a body `idempotency_key`. Without a header, the body key is used as the request key for this item. A repeat with the same key and the same values returns the first record. A repeat with the same key and different values is refused with 409.

`timestamp` must be in the period that the next invoice bills: from the start of the current billing period (or of the open pending invoice's usage window, when that is earlier) to 5 minutes after the current time. A timestamp in a period that is already invoiced, before the subscription starts, or more than 5 minutes in the future is refused with 400. The error message gives the accepted window. For a time-travelled test business, the current time is its simulated time.

Powers the business dashboard. Flow metrics (billing, payments, refunds, credit notes, signups, activations, cancellations) are bucketed by timestamp; stock metrics (MRR, CMRR, active subscriptions) are reconstructed from subscription lifecycle dates. Money is either converted into the business default currency via its manual FX rates (`currency=ALL`) or scoped to one currency.

get.description: The payments counterpart to `/analytics` (which is subscription revenue). Measures what the gateways did over a CALENDAR period resolved in the business timezone, each with its comparable previous period: gross volume, refunds, chargebacks, net volume, transaction count, successful payments, failed transactions/amount, failure rate (basis points) and pending payment intents — plus breakdowns by error cause, payment method and gateway. Same series shape as `/analytics` (`headline` + `points[]`), so one UI block consumes both. Aggregated in SQL.

get.summary: Cancellations: what they cost, why, and who left
get.description: Cancelled subscriptions whose cancellation falls in [`start`, `end`] (civil days in the business timezone), under the same filters as the subscriptions list, so each count matches the list it drills into. Each is classified by what it cost: `paying` (it lost MRR — the net of its ledger `churn` movements within a day of the cancellation), `trial_not_converted` or `no_mrr` (none to lose when it ended). Paying losses are split by `cause` (`payment_failed`, `no_payment_method` and `chargeback` are involuntary; `term_ended`; `voluntary` = no payment-related reason recorded, which on an imported cancellation says nothing either way), by merchant `reason` (`null` = none recorded), by tenure at cancellation, and over the requested `bucket`s, with the ten largest losses. Money is integer minor units per currency, plus a total in the business's default currency converted at the rate held on each cancellation day; a loss no rate reaches is counted in `totals.unconverted` and left out of the converted figures.

Null until anything has been written. `refresh_seconds` is the refresh interval.

get.summary: Every measure that can be asked for, and how it may be cut
get.description:
Discovery. Read this instead of hard-coding a list of metrics: a measure that is not here does not exist, and new ones appear here before anything else announces them.

Each entry says what the number MEANS, whether it is a value at an instant (`kind: stock`) or a sum over a window (`kind: flow`), what unit it is in, which dimensions it may be split by, which grains it may be shown at, and whether a comparison window is meaningful. A client that renders its picker from this payload cannot offer a cut the engine would refuse.

get.summary: One measure, over one window, optionally split by one dimension
get.description:
The single analytics read. Everything a chart needs is on the response and nothing has to be inferred:

- **Units are explicit.** `unit: money` is integer MINOR units in the stated `currency`; `unit: count` is a whole number; `unit: bps` is basis points. Never divide by 100 on a guess.
- **`kind` is echoed.** A `stock` is the value AT the end of each period; a `flow` is the sum ACROSS it. `total_basis` says which rule produced `total` — `value_at_end` or `sum_over_window`.
- **Freshness travels with the data**: `as_of` is when the answer was assembled, `computed_at` is when the OLDEST figure in it was computed.
- **A distinct count or cohort rate over a non-calendar window** (new customers, retention, customer churn over `range=30d` or a custom range) is computed for that exact window — `total_basis: window`, with `total_numerator` / `total_denominator` for a rate — never as a sum of its buckets. Rolling presets are precomputed hourly; a custom range is computed on demand for one business.
- **`coverage` appears when the history is partial.** A period it lists is unknown, not zero. Plotting one as zero is how a partial series becomes a flattering chart.
- **Money is never summed across currencies.** A measure held per currency with more than one currency in the window is refused until you name one; counts are combined, and `currency_basis` says which happened.

Anything coherent but unanswerable — a measure that cannot be cut by that dimension, a grain it does not support, a range with no periods — answers **422 with a sentence naming the fix**.

parameters.name: measure
parameters.description: The measure id, as listed by `GET /v1/analytics/measures` — e.g. `mrr`, `mrr_new`, `active_subscriptions`. An unknown id is a 422 naming the discovery endpoint.

parameters.name: grain
parameters.description: How finely the window is cut into periods, independently of how far back it reaches. Weeks start on the business's `week_start` (default Sunday); quarters and years follow its `fiscal_year_start_month` and are labelled by fiscal year when it is not January ("Q1 FY2027", "FY2027" — named by the year the fiscal year ends in). The first and last period are clipped to the window, so a month in progress ends today rather than at its calendar end. At organization scope the businesses' shared calendar is used, or the default when they differ.

parameters.name: range
parameters.description: A named window. With `business`, it is cut on that business's local dates. Without it, each business's figures stay on its own local dates and the window ends on the last day EVERY business has reached, so a total never mixes one business's today with another's yesterday; the returned `timezone` is then the organization's, a label. The resolved `start`, `end`, `timezone` and `timezone_source` come back on the response. `this_quarter` and `this_year` run from the start of the current FISCAL quarter/year. Mutually exclusive with `start`/`end`.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: First day of an explicit window, `YYYY-MM-DD`, inclusive. Requires `end` and excludes `range`.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: Last day of an explicit window, `YYYY-MM-DD`, inclusive. Requires `start` and excludes `range`.

parameters.name: split
parameters.description: Cut the measure by one dimension — e.g. `plan`, `plan_at_start`, `country`, `region` (UN M49 groups), `billing_interval`, `signup_cohort` (`YYYY-MM` of first payment), `currency` or `business`, subject to what that measure supports (see `dimensions` on the discovery payload). A missing value is its own `none` row, so slices sum to the total. A dimension the measure does not carry is refused by name rather than answered with an empty breakdown.

parameters.name: split_limit
parameters.description: How many split rows to return. The rows come back biggest-first by magnitude with ties broken by key, and everything beyond the limit is folded into one explicit row with `kind: truncated` — so a split can never return unbounded rows. A separate row with `kind: unattributed` carries any part of the population the dimension does not describe, whether or not anything was truncated; read `exhaustive` for whether the rows add back up to `total`.

parameters.name: currency
parameters.description: ISO 4217 code to state the figures in. Nothing is converted here: this SELECTS the currency the figures were recorded in. Omit it when only one currency is present; a money measure with several is refused until you name one.

parameters.name: compare
parameters.description: Add the equal-length window immediately before this one, as `compare` on the response: its dates, its total, the absolute change and the change in basis points. Refused on a measure whose `supports_compare` is false.

parameters.name: segment
parameters.description: A saved customer segment's id (`seg_…`, as `GET /v1/businesses/{biz}/customer_segments` lists it): the measure for that population only, computed from the MRR movement ledger. Membership is the segment as it stands TODAY, applied to all of history. Needs `business`, cannot be combined with `split`, and is accepted only where discovery marks `segmentable`.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: `series` (default) sends every period; `totals` sends the same answer with the periods left out — `series` and each split row's `points` empty, every `total` unchanged. A split then reads as a ranked list, and a measure without one as a single figure.

parameters.name: business
parameters.description: Answer for ONE business (`biz_…`). A filter, not a different question — omit it and the same measure is answered across every business in the organization, which is also what `split=business` breaks down.

422.description: A refusal with a sentence: unknown measure, unsupported dimension or grain, a range with no periods, or money in more than one currency

post.summary: Record an offline/manual payment (or mark-paid)
post.description: A debit still in progress on the invoice is cancelled at its gateway first, so the payer does not pay twice. If the gateway does not cancel it, the payment is refused with a 409.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key

date.description: When the money arrived, if not now. The payment, its transaction, its ledger postings and the invoice's `paid_at` carry it. Not in the future, not before the invoice was raised.

reference.description: The payer's reference (cheque number, wire reference). Stored as the transaction's `id_at_gateway`.

comment.description: Operator note, kept as a comment on the invoice.

shortfall.description: When `amount_minor` is less than the amount due, for this call only. `write_off`: the rest is written off with an adjustment credit note and the invoice is paid; it must fit the business limit (`billing_rules_config.partial_payment_write_off` for the currency and `partial_payment_write_off_max_percent` of the total), else the call is refused with a 400 and nothing is recorded. `leave_due`: the rest stays due. Omitted: the business rule (written off when it fits the limit). No effect when nothing is left due.

excess.description: When `amount_minor` is more than the amount due. `credit` (default): the rest is kept as the customer's excess credit (`excess_credited_minor`). `refund`: the rest is recorded as returned to the payer by the same offline method, as a succeeded `refund` transaction (`excess_refunded_minor`). The default is `credit` whatever `payment_application.excess_payment` says: that rule is for gateway payments.

post.description: The deliberate counterpart to auto-application. Unlike automatic application it does NOT consult the business's Credits Flexibility settings or the subscription's max usage fields — those govern what the engine may do unprompted. Post `{}` to apply as much refundable, then excess, as the invoice can absorb; `amount_minor` caps the total across both buckets; `refundable_minor` / `excess_minor` name exact amounts per bucket (and are refused, not clamped, if they exceed the bucket balance or the invoice's outstanding balance). Promotional credit is pre-tax and cannot be applied here.

post.summary: Estimate a change, add and/or removal (proration + tax, dry-run)
post.description: No writes. Prices modified lines, added items and removals in ONE preview, so a confirmation screen can state the whole amount that will move. A change can raise TWO documents — a proration invoice and a credit note — so `total_minor` is the DIFFERENCE between them (negative when the customer is credited) and is NOT `subtotal_minor + tax_minor`: `tax_minor`/`tax_lines` describe the invoice only, and the note’s own tax is in `credit_note_total_minor`. The note is spent in order: first relieving whatever the term's own invoices are still OWED (`credit_applied_to_open_invoices_minor` — the customer's debt is cancelled rather than refunded), then against this invoice, and only what is left over is `refundable_credit_added_minor`, which goes back on the balance. On a fully-paid term the first slice is absent and the note simply exceeds the invoice. `next_renewal` prices the NEXT renewal invoice as it will look after this change (tax and coupons in, that credit applied) so a confirmation screen never has to sum line amounts itself. On an in-trial subscription nothing is charged now: `amount_due_minor` is 0, `due_at_trial_end` is set, `next_renewal` is null, and the lines describe the full post-change composition the trial-end invoice will raise.

400.description: Invalid change, or a coupon the apply would refuse: not yet valid, expired, at its redemption limit, or used by this customer as often as it allows

post.summary: Estimate a cancellation’s money effects (dry-run)
post.description: No writes. Prices all four money effects of `POST …/cancel` under a given option set: the unbilled charges it would invoice or delete, the credit for the unused part of the term, what happens to still-open invoices, and which refundable credit notes would be refunded. Omitted options are resolved from the business defaults exactly as the cancel resolves them, so an empty body previews the cancellation you get by confirming with nothing selected. `warnings` names anything that will NOT happen the way the option set implies — most importantly, an `end_of_term` cancellation runs no credit, open-invoice or refund step. At the term end it only raises a final invoice for the term's metered usage and pending unbilled charges, and it ignores every other option.

post.summary: Estimate a reactivation's first invoice (dry-run)
post.description:
No writes. Prices the FRESH FULL TERM that `POST …/reactivate` would bill for a CANCELLED subscription, through the same rating, tax vector and customer-balance draw the booking uses — lines, `subtotal_minor`, `discount_minor`, named `tax_lines[]`, `total_minor` (the invoice), `credits_applied_minor` and `amount_due_minor` (what is actually collected). Refused with 400 unless the subscription is `cancelled`, or when `coupon_code` is one the apply would refuse: not yet valid, expired, at its redemption limit, or used by this customer as often as the coupon allows.

Distinct from `…/estimate`, which prorates against a CURRENT TERM a cancelled subscription does not have, and from `…/customers/{cus}/subscription_estimate`, which knows no subscription and so cannot apply that subscription's own `max_refundable_credits_usage_minor`.

`items` is REQUIRED: this prices the item set you are previewing. `trial_end` is accepted because it changes the money — nothing is collected today, so `amount_due_minor` is 0 and `due_at_trial_end` says when the conversion bills instead. `billing_cycles` and `charges_handling` are NOT accepted: neither changes the first invoice's composition (a cycle cap bites from the second cycle, and `charges_handling` decides whether this composition is invoiced or parked as an unbilled charge), so accepting them would imply the preview varies with them.

When the reactivation continues the current term (see `POST …/reactivate`), `in_term_reactivation` is set: `current_period_end`, the term's `invoice` with its `outstanding_minor`, and `collects_now`. Lines and totals are then 0, and `amount_due_minor` is what collecting that invoice takes now (0 unless `collects_now`). `in_term_available` is on every reactivation estimate: whether `term: continue` is possible for these items, so a screen can offer the choice after `term: new` is selected.

post.summary: Reactivate (clear pending cancel, or restart a canceled sub)
post.description:
An empty body clears a pending cancellation, or restarts a cancelled subscription on its items. Any field below restarts it with those options. The fresh term is invoiced and collected unless `trial_end` or `charges_handling: add_to_unbilled_charges` defers it; with auto-collection on, a failed charge refuses the reactivation when `on_charge_failure` resolves to `refuse` (402), and anything this call applied is taken back off.

In-term reactivation: a subscription that dunning cancelled (`cancel_reason` `no_card` or `not_paid`) and whose term has not ended continues that term when the request keeps its items, sets no `trial_end`, `reactivate_from` or payment fields, and does not send `term: new`. No invoice is raised and the term's invoice keeps its balance. When `on_charge_failure` resolves to `refuse` and auto-collection is on, that invoice is collected once first, and a failure refuses the reactivation (402).

get.description: Every report this business can answer, as DECLARATIONS — key, name, description, category and its label, cross-cutting tags, the dimensions it may be grouped by, and its variants. A client renders a report it has never heard of from this plus the answer envelope, which is the point: a catalogue with its own copy of what exists will eventually offer a report the engine has dropped, or hide one it has gained.

get.description:
One report, in the uniform envelope every key returns: a headline, a series (`points`), and — depending on the report's shape — `rows` for a breakdown, `matrix` for a cohort grid, or `table` for a reconciling waterfall. `format=csv` returns the SAME answer as a file, from the same resolver, so the download and the screen cannot disagree.

`granularity` is independent of `range`: it re-cuts the preset's own span rather than widening it, and is REFUSED with a 400 — never ignored — on any shape with no series to re-cut, because honouring it silently would let a reader believe a table had been re-cut. `group_by` is likewise refused unless the report declares that dimension. Where a report supports a previous-period comparison it declares `comparable` and its answer carries one, including the BASIS the pair was cut on — a partial period is never compared against a complete one.

parameters.name: aging_interval
parameters.description: How wide the receivables ageing ladder's rungs are, in days. `standard` (the default) is the ladder as it has always been: monthly rungs to six months, then one rung to a year. A number gives uniform rungs of that many days out to a year, the last rung absorbing the remainder, then the same open-ended tail. Each rung NAME carries its own boundaries, so a row printed at any interval drills into the invoices behind it through the same `ar_bucket` filter. Refused with a 400 — never ignored — on a report that is not an ageing ladder, and on a width outside the set above. The catalogue's `aging_intervals` says which reports take it.

get.summary: The rows behind a report figure
get.description:
A report says the quarter billed $1.44M; this says which invoices, movements, payments or refunds. Reconciling with the figure is the whole point, so the window is taken from the report layer's own bucket builder rather than re-derived from the range name — cut on a second calendar, an export would explain a number it does not equal. Σ `reporting_amount_minor` over the window equals the headline of the dataset's `reconciles_with` report, exactly, in integer minor units.

Every money column stays in the currency it was earned in, with `reporting_rate` and `reporting_amount_minor` beside it saying what conversion the report applied. Totals are offered PER CURRENCY and never across them: adding paise to cents produces a number that is true of nothing. A row in a currency no exchange rate reaches is left out, because the report leaves it out too.

`data` is an array of arrays positioned by `columns`, paged with the usual `limit`/`starting_after` cursor. `format=csv` streams the same rows a page at a time, so the response is bounded by a page rather than by the size of the tenant; an empty window still returns the header row, because a file with no header reads as a broken export rather than a quiet period.

post.summary: Register a storefront domain for wallet buttons
post.description: Apple Pay will not render its button on a domain the gateway has not registered, and it fails SILENTLY — no error, no console warning, no failed request — so an unregistered domain is indistinguishable from no support at all. Nothing else is needed for wallets: an Apple Pay token is a card credential, Stripe's PaymentElement surfaces the button on its own, and a saved instrument reads back as `Apple Pay` rather than a bare card brand. Registering re-validates every time, because a domain registered before its association file was in place stays inactive until something asks again. The per-wallet `active` flags and any `detail` are the GATEWAY's verdict, not ours — `detail` usually names the real cause, which is that `/.well-known/apple-developer-merchantid-domain-association` is not reachable on that domain. Safe to repeat: a domain the gateway already knows reports its status instead of erroring. Gateways with no such concept answer 409.

OMIT IT in the normal case: the domain that matters is the STOREFRONT's, which this deployment already names in `PORTAL_BASE_URL`, and in production that is a different host from the dashboard (`portal.…` vs `app.…`). Registering the dashboard's domain succeeds and leaves the wallet dark, which is the hardest failure of all to diagnose. Pass one only to override. 400 if it is omitted and no `PORTAL_BASE_URL` is set.

Creates the intent AND its first attempt; the response carries `attempt`, because the buyer’s challenge (`next_action`) belongs to that attempt.

**`purpose: payment`** — requires `payment_method` and a positive `amount_minor`. The customer comes from the payment method, so `customer` must be omitted.

post.summary: Replay a gateway webhook whose processing failed
post.description:
Re-runs reconciliation for a webhook left at `outcome: error` or `outcome: ignored`. A failed event is answered 502 and also retried by us, independent of the gateway: about 25 tries over about 4 days. If the last try fails, the webhook's `error` ends with a note that automatic retries stopped, and this call runs it again.

A `processed` row never replays: re-running it would re-execute handlers that book money. A replay that finds the event already settled by a concurrent retry answers `duplicate`. The signature is NOT re-verified and cannot be (stored headers are redacted and the raw bytes are gone), so this consumes the normalized event recorded at ingest — the row exists only because verification passed then. Events from before that field existed are refused with 409.

A `SubscriptionConfirmation` is confirmed automatically, but only AFTER the signature verifies, since the callback URL is attacker-supplied otherwise. put.summary: Set one currency's exchange-rate source (manual rate, or auto-refreshed)
put.description:
The **Manage currency** dialog: a currency's rate is either typed in and left alone (`manual`) or refreshed daily from a provider (`auto`).

A per-currency sub-resource on purpose. Switching INR to auto says nothing about EUR, whereas sending a partial `exchange_rates` map on the business patch would be ambiguous between *leave the others* and *delete them*.

`auto` attempts ONE provider fetch inline, so the response carries the rate the screen is about to show. **A failed fetch is still a 200**: the currency is recorded as auto, the previous rate stands, and `last_error` says why it did not move — read `updated_at` and `last_error` to tell a refreshed rate from a kept one. The daily job retries. Rates are reporting-only and never rate or settle a charge, whatever their source.

The business's own default currency is refused (400): it is 1 against itself by definition, and a settable rate for it would invite someone to set it to something else.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Safely retry writes — repeats return the original response. If a write FAILED after it had already taken effect, that failure is what repeats: the key is spent, and a new attempt needs a new key.

source.description: Where the rate comes from: `manual` or `auto`.

rate.description: Units of this currency per 1 unit of the default currency, > 0. Send a STRING to keep your own precision — `94.9537410` survives as typed, where a JSON number may not.

source.description: Where the rate comes from: `manual` or `auto`.

oneOf.description: No `rate` — one sent with `auto` would be overwritten by the next refresh, so it is rejected rather than silently discarded.

400.description: Not a positive rate, a `rate` sent with `auto`, or the business's own default currency

delete.summary: Stop transacting in a currency (drops its rate too)
delete.description:
Removes the currency from the business's enabled list AND deletes its rate and provenance — both halves, because either alone leaves something untrue behind: an orphaned rate the daily refresh keeps updating and no screen shows, or a sellable currency with nothing to convert it by.

Prices and invoices already in that currency are UNTOUCHED. An invoice carries its own `exchange_rate` snapshot, so historical conversion survives the live rate being deleted — that is what the snapshot is for.

The business's own default currency is refused (400): every other rate is quoted against it. Change the default first.

fiscal_year_start_month.description: The month (1–12) this business's fiscal year starts in; 1 is the calendar year. Analytics quarters, years, `this_quarter` and `this_year` follow it, and a fiscal year is named by the calendar year it ends in (April 2026 – March 2027 is FY2027, its first quarter "Q1 FY2027"). Changing it re-computes the stored quarterly and yearly figures in the background.
